body:
Why Gujarat has an industrial advantage

The value of green hydrogen depends not only on producing it but also on finding industries that need it. Gujarat has a strong combination of renewable electricity resources, petroleum refineries, fertilizer and chemical industries, ports and transport infrastructure.

This creates an opportunity to connect renewable electricity generation with existing hydrogen demand and new industries producing green ammonia or other hydrogen-derived chemicals.

Important industrial locations

LocationIndustrial or geographical importanceGreen-hydrogen opportunity
JamnagarMajor petroleum refining and petrochemical centre in SaurashtraPotential replacement of conventional refinery hydrogen
VadinarPetroleum refining and coastal infrastructure in Devbhumi Dwarka districtRefinery hydrogen and industrial energy applications
Koyali, near VadodaraLocation of the Gujarat RefineryIndustrial use of low-emission hydrogen
Dahej, Bharuch districtMajor chemical, petrochemical and port-based industrial areaGreen ammonia, chemicals and industrial hydrogen use
Hazira, Surat districtMajor industrial and port areaIndustrial consumption and hydrogen-related manufacturing

These are industrial opportunities, not a claim that every refinery or factory listed has already converted its hydrogen supply to green hydrogen. An operational facility must be distinguished from a proposed investment, announced project or future demand estimate.

Why ports are central to the hydrogen economy

Ports are important because they connect industrial production with domestic shipping and international trade. Hydrogen-derived products such as ammonia may require specialized storage tanks, dedicated loading arrangements, handling systems and safety procedures.

Gujarat's port-industrial geography is particularly useful:

  • Deendayal Port at Kandla: Located in Kachchh and connected with a major industrial and logistics region.
  • Mundra: A major port in Kachchh with opportunities associated with industrial logistics and renewable-energy-linked manufacturing.
  • Dahej: A port-industrial area in Bharuch district, associated with the Gulf of Khambhat and chemical industries.
  • Hazira: A port and industrial area in Surat district with substantial industrial activity.

Port access is an advantage, but it does not itself establish that a green-hydrogen export industry is operating at commercial scale. Production, product quality, storage, shipping agreements and demand must also exist.

Deendayal Port's recognised status

On 10 October 2025, the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy formally recognised 3 major port areas as Green Hydrogen Hubs under the National Green Hydrogen Mission:

  • Deendayal Port Authority, Kandla, Gujarat.
  • V.O. Chidambaranar Port Authority, Tamil Nadu.
  • Paradip Port Authority, Odisha.

The purpose of a hub is to bring production, consumption, transport and other infrastructure into a common industrial area. The recognition can facilitate access to benefits under applicable schemes, but recognition under the relevant provision does not itself guarantee direct financial assistance.

The Deendayal Port Authority commissioned an indigenously built 1 MW green-hydrogen plant in July 2025. This is an example of a facility that moved beyond an announcement into commissioning.

In a government report dated 28 March 2026, the port was also reported to have allotted approximately 3,400 acres to developers for green-hydrogen and green-ammonia projects. Land allotment is a development step; it must not be interpreted as completed production capacity.

Connecting Kachchh's renewable electricity to industry

A possible Gujarat green-hydrogen development chain begins with renewable generation in Kachchh or other suitable regions. Electricity is supplied to an electrolyser, which produces hydrogen from purified water. The hydrogen can be consumed by a nearby industrial plant or converted into another chemical product. Green ammonia can then be stored and potentially shipped through a suitable port.

This chain explains why green-hydrogen development is not simply a question of choosing the sunniest location. An industrial cluster with reliable electricity supply, water management, transport facilities and an existing customer may be more practical than a remote location with excellent sunlight but no nearby demand.

Exports and import substitution

Green hydrogen can reduce the need for some fossil-derived hydrogen in existing industries. This is a form of industrial import substitution or decarbonisation, depending on the original source of the fuel and feedstock.

Green ammonia and other hydrogen derivatives also create potential export opportunities where overseas customers require lower-emission industrial materials or fuels. Export competitiveness depends on production cost, international standards, shipping arrangements and market demand. Gujarat's ports provide geographical advantages, but commercial exports cannot be inferred merely from an export proposal.

Prelims focus

  • Jamnagar and Vadinar are important petroleum refining locations in Gujarat.
  • Dahej is in Bharuch district; Hazira is in Surat district.
  • Deendayal Port is located at Kandla in Kachchh.
  • Deendayal, V.O. Chidambaranar and Paradip were recognised as Green Hydrogen Hubs in October 2025.
  • A 1 MW green-hydrogen plant was commissioned at Kandla in July 2025.
  • Trap: Port-hub recognition or land allotment does not mean all proposed hydrogen production and export facilities have been commissioned.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Mineral and Energy Resources and Manufacturing Industries chapters; Press Information Bureau, Three Major Ports Recognised as Green Hydrogen Hubs under National Green Hydrogen Mission, 10 October 2025; Press Information Bureau, Indigenously-Built 1 MW Green Hydrogen Plant Commissioned at Kandla Port, 31 July 2025; Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, parliamentary reply on Green Hydrogen Hubs, 28 March 2026, Deendayal Port Authority annexure; Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, National Green Hydrogen Mission, industrial demand and export objectives; official sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
Renewable energy still requires natural resources

Solar and wind electricity generally avoid the direct combustion emissions associated with fossil-fuel electricity generation. However, renewable-energy systems are not completely free from environmental effects. They require land or marine space, equipment, access roads, transmission connections and materials for construction.

A project should therefore be evaluated for its expected reduction in emissions and its local effects on water, biodiversity, livelihoods and other land uses.

Land use in Kachchh and Saurashtra

Large ground-mounted solar installations need considerable space. Wind turbines may occupy smaller individual foundations, but wind farms also require access roads, electricity lines and adequate spacing between turbines.

In Kachchh and Saurashtra, proposed sites may overlap with grazing land, seasonal wetlands, agricultural land, saline ecosystems or areas used by local communities. An apparently dry or sparsely vegetated landscape can still support important ecological processes and livelihoods.

Rooftop, canal-top and some other distributed solar installations can reduce the need to occupy additional open land. However, their own technical, maintenance and cost limitations must be considered.

Biodiversity and wildlife protection

Biodiversity includes variation among living organisms and the ecosystems in which they occur. Renewable projects can affect biodiversity through habitat change, disturbance, road construction, electricity lines or other infrastructure.

Gujarat's ecological concerns include:

  • Kachchh's wetlands and saline habitats: Seasonal water bodies, open landscapes and associated habitats can support migratory birds and other wildlife.
  • Grassland birds: Large birds such as the Great Indian Bustard are vulnerable to certain infrastructure risks, including collisions with overhead power lines in relevant habitats.
  • Gulf of Kachchh marine habitats: The gulf contains coral reefs, mangroves and marine wildlife. The Marine National Park and Marine Sanctuary are especially important protected coastal ecosystems.
  • Coastal livelihoods: Offshore and port-related projects may affect fishing access, navigation, coastal habitats and marine activities.

Project suitability depends on the exact location. It would be incorrect to assume that all renewable installations in Kachchh damage protected wildlife areas; it would also be incorrect to assume that no ecological restrictions apply because a project is renewable.

Water requirements and desalination

Water is another important consideration in Gujarat's drier regions. Solar modules may require cleaning, although water-efficient and dry-cleaning methods can reduce consumption.

Green hydrogen has a more direct water requirement. Approximately 9 litres of purified water per kg of hydrogen is the theoretical chemical input for water electrolysis. Water used in purification, cooling and other operations may make the total requirement higher.

Where a coastal green-hydrogen plant uses seawater, desalination removes dissolved salts, and further treatment prepares the water for electrolysis. Desalination can reduce dependence on scarce inland freshwater, but it consumes energy and produces a saline reject stream. Brine disposal needs appropriate management to limit marine environmental harm.

Understanding the main trade-offs

Technology or activityImportant benefitImportant limitation
Ground-mounted solarElectricity without fuel combustion during operationLand occupation, variable output and site-specific ecological effects
Rooftop solarGeneration close to electricity useLimited suitable roof area and daytime variability
Onshore windCan generate during daylight and darknessVariable wind conditions and possible bird or habitat impacts
Offshore windUses marine wind resourcesMarine construction, fisheries, ecological and transmission challenges
Battery storageShifts electricity from one period to anotherInitial cost, finite storage duration and material requirements
Green hydrogenCan replace fossil-derived hydrogen in some industriesRequires renewable energy, purified water and additional conversion processes

Why cost depends on the whole system

The cost of renewable electricity is influenced by the quality of the resource, equipment prices, construction, operation, land arrangements and grid connectivity. A location with strong sunlight may still be expensive to develop if transmission infrastructure is inadequate or the site presents major environmental and logistical difficulties.

The cost of green hydrogen depends strongly on the price and availability of renewable electricity and the cost and utilisation of the electrolyser. Water treatment, compression, storage and delivery add further costs. Producing green ammonia adds another industrial conversion stage and requires appropriate storage and handling.

These relationships explain why the cheapest renewable electricity location is not necessarily the cheapest location for delivering green hydrogen to a refinery or a port.

Practical environmental safeguards

Suitable development measures include careful site selection, protection of sensitive habitats, appropriate planning of transmission routes, water-efficient operation, safe disposal or treatment of waste streams, equipment recycling and consultation with affected communities.

Environmental assessment is therefore part of sustainable renewable-energy development rather than an argument against renewable energy itself.

Prelims focus

  • Renewable energy can reduce fossil-fuel emissions but is not automatically free of ecological impacts.
  • Gujarat's Gulf of Kachchh contains important coral and mangrove habitats.
  • Large birds may face collision risks from overhead electricity lines.
  • Green-hydrogen electrolysis needs purified water; desalination is a possible coastal supply option.
  • Battery storage does not create energy and introduces material and recycling considerations.
  • Trap: Dry or saline land is not necessarily ecologically empty land.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, Chapter 2, Land, Soil, Water, Natural Vegetation and Wildlife Resources, printed pp. 15-21; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, Chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 164-170; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, Biodiversity and Conservation chapter; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, National Biodiversity Action Plan implementation report, Coral Reef Conservation section; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Coastal Ecosystem Health Report Card for the Marine National Park and Sanctuary, Jamnagar, 2024; Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board, Pathways for Transmission of Hydrogen in India, 2025, Water Availability section; sources consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Land, Water, Biodiversity and Cost: Environmental Trade-offs of Gujarat's Energy Transition
